title: My God, why (Psalm 21 [22])
hookLine: the psalm Jesus prayed from the cross, which ends in praise

cards: Good Friday, the ninth hour. Jesus has been on the cross since morning. The sky has gone dark.

Then, the Gospels say, he cries out with a loud voice, in his own language, words bystanders mishear. Matthew writes them down: "Eli, Eli, lamma sabacthani? that is, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"
For two thousand years, people have stopped at that sentence. It sounds like the bottom of the world. But anyone there who knew the psalms would have recognized it.
He wasn't inventing those words. He was praying them.

teach.h: A PSALM NAMED BY ITS FIRST LINE.
teach.b: They're the first line of Psalm 21 in the Douay, 22 in most Bibles: "O God my God, look upon me: why hast thou forsaken me?"

In the ancient world, a psalm was often named by its first line, the way we'd name a song by its opening words. So many readers hear Jesus calling up the whole psalm. Its first half is as dark as scripture gets.
The one praying is mocked; people shake their heads and say, let God rescue him, then.
He's poured out like water, his bones out of joint, his heart like melting wax, his tongue stuck to his jaw.

teach.h: THEY CAST LOTS FOR HIS VESTURE.
teach.b: "They parted my garments amongst them; and upon my vesture they cast lots." The Gospels tell that very thing happening at the foot of the cross, and John quotes the line.
Then, near the end, the psalm stops asking why and starts thanking. God has not despised the poor man's cry. The poor will eat and be filled.
All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord, and people not yet born will be told what God has done. It begins in abandonment and ends with the whole world praising.

Christians have thought for centuries about how to understand Jesus praying this. The Church holds both at once: he truly felt the full weight of that cry, and he prayed it as a psalm of trust whose ending he knew.
Either way, the words were given to anyone who has ever felt forsaken.

how: Catholics hear Psalm 21 [22] as the responsorial psalm on Palm Sunday, just before the Passion is read, and pray it in the Liturgy of the Hours; many pray its first line in times of desolation.

games.q: you've read the first half of Psalm 21 and it's as dark as it gets. keep reading. where does it go?
o: deeper into despair, and it stops there.

games.why: near the end it stops asking why and starts thanking: the poor will eat and be filled, and the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord.

practice: Bring to mind one person who feels abandoned right now, grieving, sick, lonely, far from home or far from God, and without trying to fix it, stand next to them in your mind.
If you pray, say the psalm's first line for them, honestly, the way Jesus did: my God, my God, why? If you don't, simply hold them in your attention.

wordCard.voice: My God. The cry that opens Psalm 21, prayed by Jesus from the cross, from a psalm that begins forsaken and ends in praise. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: my God, my God, why have you forsaken me? the Gospels give it in Aramaic form, sabachthani.

carryVoice: Your line: even this is prayer. A why, said honestly, still counts. See you tomorrow.
